title: ‘My Fourth Child’: The End of a Ten-Year Partnership
text:
Khachanov Parts Ways With Coach Martic After 10 Years

 Karen Khachanov Splits With Coach Vedran Martic After a Decade 
 ATP Tour Karen Khachanov Splits With Coach Vedran Martic After a Decade 
 Jim Flannigan | 20 October 2026 | 3 min read Karen Khachanov - Photo: IMAGO / Xinhua Share this article
 Add us as a preferred source on Google Karen Khachanov announced on Monday that he has ended his long-term working relationship with Croatian coach Vedran Martic, posting the news directly to his Instagram just days after the curtain came down on the Shanghai Masters. Andrey Chesnokov, the former Soviet-era top-10 player, will step in for the remainder of the 2026 season.
 A partnership that shaped a career
 The numbers behind this split deserve a moment. Ten years is an eternity in professional tennis, where coaching arrangements routinely dissolve mid-tournament, let alone mid-decade. Martic was with Khachanov across two stints, guiding him from a raw teenage prospect into a genuine force at the top of the game. Their work together produced seven ATP Tour singles titles, including a Masters 1000 at the 2018 Paris Masters. It also delivered a career-high ranking of No. 8, reached in July 2019.
 The bond went well beyond tactics and fitness work. Martic had described Khachanov as his fourth child, a rare level of personal closeness in a sport where the player-coach relationship is usually framed in purely professional terms. That context makes the timing of the split, mid-season and announced via social media rather than through any formal press conference, all the more striking.
 The decision was taken by mutual agreement, according to reports citing Khachanov’s own social media post.
 A difficult year behind him, a fresh start ahead
 The 2026 season had a strange arc for Khachanov. He struggled badly through the spring and summer clay and grass swings, at one point switching back to his old racket model on the eve of the US Open after weeks of fighting his technique. The change worked. He reached the US Open semifinals, where he lost to Alexander Zverev 6-3, 7-6, 7-6. A run to the final four of a major at 30 years old is not the form of a player coasting. Whether those results factored into the decision to reconfigure his team anyway is not clear from the announcement.
 The replacement signals an intent to keep things close to home. Andrey Chesnokov is a Russian tennis player and coach who was one of the most consistent clay-court performers the Soviet Union and then Russia produced in the late 1980s and early 1990s, reaching the Monte Carlo final as recently as 1990. At 60, he brings a depth of competitive experience that few coaches in the game can match, along with an understanding of Russian tennis culture that should ease the transition.
 What the change means going forward
 The practical challenge is timing. With the season effectively in its final weeks, Chesnokov has almost no runway to implement anything structural before the year ends. The appointment is essentially a holding arrangement, a chance for both men to assess whether the fit is right before committing to a full 2027 campaign.
 For Khachanov, the stakes around that decision are real. He currently sits at No. 27 in the world. He has been in and around the top 30 for most of the past four years, but the gap between that and the top 10 he once occupied has proved stubborn. The Paris Masters, where he won his biggest title eight years ago and where he carries strong emotional currency, is the obvious near-term target to judge whether the new arrangement brings any early spark.
 Martic, for his part, exits with an exceptional record. Coaching one player for a decade in this sport is rare. Coaching them to seven titles, three major semifinals, an Olympic silver medal and a top-10 peak is rarer still. The parting was mutual and professional. The next move on his side will be worth watching.
 Written by
 Jim Flannigan
 Jim Flannigan is a tennis journalist and analyst. A competitive player until injury ended his playing career, he studied at the University of Leeds and has spent 16 years covering the sport as a freelancer. He writes primarily on Tenniswatcher.
